questions.stem: Which of the following is a gain from international trade for Australian consumers?
options: A greater choice of goods and services at lower prices
Protection of local firms and jobs from overseas competition
Higher prices for imported goods and services
Reduced access to resources that Australia lacks
questions.explanation: Trade lets Australians buy goods made more cheaply elsewhere and widens the range of products available. Protecting local firms from competition is the opposite of the gains trade brings.

questions.stem: Selling into large overseas markets lets Australian firms produce at higher volumes and lower average costs. This gain from trade is known as:
options: a trade-weighted gain
economies of scale
the terms of trade
the substitution effect
questions.explanation: Economies of scale are the falls in average cost that come with larger output. Access to world markets lets firms grow beyond the size the domestic market alone would support.

questions.stem: Exposure to import competition can raise the efficiency of Australian firms because:
options: firms must cut costs and innovate to keep their customers
imports raise local prices, so domestic firms earn more profit to invest
governments subsidise any firm that faces competition from imports
it reduces the range of products from which consumers can choose
questions.explanation: When consumers can buy imports, local firms that are inefficient lose sales, so they must lower costs and improve their products. This is the competition and efficiency gain from trade.

questions.stem: Australia imports most of its refined fuel and many advanced machines. This mainly illustrates which gain from international trade?
options: Higher prices paid by domestic consumers for imported products
An improvement in the terms of trade from higher export prices
Access to resources and goods not readily produced locally
Economies of scale achieved in Australia's domestic refining industry
questions.explanation: Trade gives Australia access to goods and inputs it cannot produce, or cannot produce as cheaply, at home. Those imports support both consumption and production.

questions.stem: The balance of payments records:
options: the total stock of foreign debt owed by Australian residents at a particular date in time
the federal government's budget transactions with overseas governments each year
the value of goods exported and imported, excluding services and financial flows
all transactions between Australian residents and the rest of the world over a period
questions.explanation: The balance of payments is a record of flows over a period, covering trade in goods and services, income, transfers, and capital and financial transactions. Foreign debt is a stock, recorded separately in the international investment position.

questions.stem: The current account of the balance of payments consists of:
options: the balance on goods and services, the primary income balance and the secondary income balance
the capital account, the financial account and the net errors and omissions item
direct investment, portfolio investment, financial derivatives and reserve assets
net foreign debt, net foreign equity and the net international investment position
questions.explanation: The current account records trade in goods and services, primary income such as interest and dividends, and secondary income such as transfers. Direct and portfolio investment belong in the financial account.

questions.stem: Interest paid by Australian companies to foreign lenders is recorded in the balance of payments as:
options: a credit in the primary income account
a debit in the financial account
a debit in the secondary income account
a debit in the primary income account
questions.explanation: Interest and dividends paid to and received from overseas are primary income flows. A payment to non-residents is a debit, so interest paid abroad adds to a primary income deficit.

questions.stem: Money sent home by migrant workers in Australia to their families overseas is recorded as:
options: a credit in the financial account
an import in the goods and services account
a debit in the secondary income account
a debit in the primary income account
questions.explanation: Personal transfers are made without anything being received in return, so they are secondary income. Money leaving Australia is a debit.

questions.stem: A Japanese company buys a controlling share in an Australian mining company. This transaction is recorded as:
options: a credit in the financial account, as direct investment
a debit in the financial account, as portfolio investment
a credit in the current account, as an export
a credit in the primary income account, as income
questions.explanation: Foreign purchase of a controlling stake is direct investment, and funds flowing into Australia are recorded as a credit in the financial account. Any future dividends paid to the Japanese owner will appear as primary income debits.

questions.stem: International students paying tuition fees to Australian universities are recorded as:
options: a credit in the goods and services account, as an export of services
a debit in the goods and services account, as an import of services
a credit in the financial account, as foreign investment
a credit in the secondary income account, as a transfer
questions.explanation: Education sold to non-residents is an export of services, even though it is delivered in Australia. Exports earn money from overseas, so they are credits.

questions.stem: Australia has a current account deficit of $30 billion and net errors and omissions are zero. The capital and financial account must show:
options: a surplus of $60 billion
a surplus of $30 billion
a deficit of $30 billion
a balance of zero
questions.explanation: The balance of payments always balances, so the current account and the capital and financial account sum to zero. A $30 billion current account deficit must be matched by a $30 billion net inflow of capital.

questions.stem: In a hypothetical quarter, the goods and services balance is +$12 billion, the primary income balance is −$18 billion and the secondary income balance is −$1 billion. The current account balance is:
options: a deficit of $7 billion
a surplus of $7 billion
a deficit of $5 billion
a surplus of $29 billion
questions.explanation: Adding the three balances gives 12 − 18 − 1 = −7, a deficit of $7 billion. Treating the secondary income balance as positive would give −5 instead.

questions.stem: Australia has a long history of deficits on the primary income account, mainly because:
options: it has usually imported a greater value of goods and services than it has exported overseas
it sends large amounts of foreign aid to developing countries in the region each year
foreign tourists spend less in Australia than Australian tourists spend overseas
it has relied on foreign capital, so it pays interest and dividends to foreign investors
questions.explanation: Decades of borrowing and equity investment from overseas mean large flows of interest and dividends to non-residents, which are primary income debits. Trade in goods and services and tourism are recorded in a different part of the current account.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a cyclical influence on Australia's current account balance?
options: The accumulated stock of Australia's foreign liabilities
A narrow export base concentrated in mining and agriculture
A rise in world commodity prices that lifts export income
A long-run gap between national saving and investment
questions.explanation: Cyclical influences change with economic conditions, such as commodity prices, the exchange rate and the business cycle here and overseas. The saving-investment gap, the stock of foreign liabilities and the export base are long-standing structural features.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a structural influence on Australia's current account balance?
options: A cyclical upswing in the growth of Australia's major trading partners
A drought that reduces farm exports for one season
Australia's long-standing reliance on foreign saving to fund investment
A temporary fall in the value of the Australian dollar over a few months
questions.explanation: Structural influences are persistent features of the economy, such as investment exceeding national saving and the resulting payments on foreign capital. Short-lived changes in the dollar, overseas growth or the weather are cyclical.

questions.stem: A strong upswing in Australian domestic demand, with no change overseas, is most likely to cause the current account balance to:
options: stay the same, as only exports affect it
deteriorate, as spending on imports rises
improve, as export volumes rise with demand
improve, as income paid to foreigners falls
questions.explanation: Higher domestic incomes and spending increase demand for imports, while export demand depends on overseas conditions, which have not changed. The goods and services balance and therefore the current account worsen.

questions.stem: When national investment exceeds national saving, the economy must:
options: run a current account surplus by lending to the rest of the world
cut government spending until the budget returns to surplus
raise interest rates above those in major overseas economies
draw on foreign saving, matched by a current account deficit
questions.explanation: Investment that is not funded from domestic saving must be financed by borrowing or equity from overseas, which is a net capital inflow. A net capital inflow is the other side of a current account deficit.

questions.stem: Net foreign debt is:
options: foreign ownership of Australian shares and property minus Australian ownership of foreign shares and property
the total amount that the Australian Government has borrowed from overseas lenders
the size of the current account deficit recorded in a single year
Australians' borrowings from the rest of the world minus Australians' lending to the rest of the world
questions.explanation: Net foreign debt is a stock of debt liabilities, netting what Australians owe overseas against what they are owed. Ownership of shares and property is equity, measured by net foreign equity.

questions.stem: Net foreign equity measures:
options: foreign ownership of Australian equity minus Australian ownership of foreign equity
the total foreign debt owed by Australians minus the portion owed by the federal government
the interest that Australian borrowers owe to foreign lenders each year
the value of Australia's exports minus the value of its imports
questions.explanation: Equity is ownership, such as shares and property. Net foreign equity compares foreign-owned equity in Australia with Australian-owned equity abroad.

questions.stem: Persistent current account deficits tend to add to Australia's net foreign liabilities because:
options: they raise Australia's export earnings from commodities over time
they lower the cost of servicing Australia's existing foreign debt
they are financed by foreign borrowing or by selling assets to foreigners
they cause the Australian dollar to appreciate against major currencies
questions.explanation: Each deficit must be funded by a net capital inflow, either debt, which adds to net foreign debt, or equity, which adds to net foreign equity. Over time the stock of liabilities builds up.

questions.stem: A rising stock of net foreign debt can worsen Australia's current account balance over time because:
options: it raises the volume of imports bought by Australian households
it lowers the world prices of Australia's commodity exports
it increases the foreign aid that Australia pays overseas
interest payments on the debt add to the primary income deficit
questions.explanation: More debt means more interest owed to non-residents, which is a primary income debit. A larger primary income deficit worsens the current account, which can then require further borrowing.

questions.stem: Australian superannuation funds increase their holdings of overseas shares, with nothing else changing. This will:
options: increase Australia's net foreign debt
reduce Australia's export income
reduce Australia's net foreign equity
increase Australia's net foreign equity
questions.explanation: Net foreign equity is foreign-owned equity in Australia minus Australian-owned equity abroad. Buying more foreign shares raises the second term, so net foreign equity falls; shares are equity, so foreign debt is unchanged.

questions.stem: The exchange rate is:
options: the rate at which imports grow over a year
the price of one currency expressed in terms of another
the interest rate charged on loans from overseas
the ratio of export prices to import prices
questions.explanation: The exchange rate tells us how much of a foreign currency one Australian dollar buys. The ratio of export to import prices is the terms of trade.

questions.stem: The trade-weighted index (TWI) measures the value of the Australian dollar:
options: against a basket of trading partners' currencies, weighted by their share of trade
against the United States dollar only, as most world trade is priced in US dollars
relative to the world price of gold, measured each trading day
against the currencies of the countries to which Australia owes debt
questions.explanation: The TWI gives a broad measure of the dollar's value by weighting each partner's currency by its importance in Australia's trade. The dollar can rise against one currency while the TWI falls.

questions.stem: The exchange rate moves from 65 US cents to 70 US cents per Australian dollar. This means the Australian dollar has:
options: depreciated, as Australian exports become cheaper in US dollars
appreciated, as US imports become dearer in Australian dollars
appreciated, as one Australian dollar now buys more US dollars
depreciated, as one Australian dollar now buys fewer US dollars
questions.explanation: Each Australian dollar now buys 70 US cents rather than 65, so its value has risen. An appreciation makes exports dearer for US buyers and imports cheaper for Australians.

questions.stem: Australian interest rates rise while overseas rates are unchanged. The Australian dollar will tend to:
options: depreciate, as investors move their funds out of Australian financial assets and into others
appreciate, as Australians buy more imports with their savings
depreciate, as overseas demand for Australian exports weakens
appreciate, as higher returns attract capital inflow and demand for the dollar
questions.explanation: Higher relative interest rates make Australian assets more attractive, so foreign investors buy Australian dollars to invest. Buying more imports would increase the supply of dollars and push the dollar down, not up.

questions.stem: A sharp rise in world iron ore prices is most likely to cause the Australian dollar to:
options: stay unchanged, as iron ore is priced in US dollars rather than Australian dollars
appreciate, as larger export earnings converted into Australian dollars raise demand for the dollar
depreciate, as Australian steelmakers must pay more for the iron ore they use in their production
appreciate, as Australians increase their demand for imported goods and services
questions.explanation: Higher commodity prices raise export income, which exporters convert into Australian dollars, increasing demand for the currency. Being priced in US dollars does not stop this, because the proceeds are still exchanged for Australian dollars.

questions.stem: Inflation in Australia runs persistently above the rate in its trading partners. Other things being equal, the Australian dollar will tend to:
options: appreciate, as Australian exports become more competitive overseas
depreciate, as demand for Australian exports falls and imports rise
appreciate, as higher Australian prices attract more foreign buyers
depreciate, as Australians buy fewer goods and services from overseas
questions.explanation: Higher relative inflation makes Australian goods dearer and imports relatively cheaper, so demand for the dollar falls and supply rises. That pushes the exchange rate down.

questions.stem: A downgrade of Australia's sovereign credit rating would most likely cause the Australian dollar to:
options: depreciate, as Australian assets become less attractive to foreign investors
appreciate, as foreign investors buy more Australian government bonds
depreciate, as Australian exports become more competitive overseas
appreciate, as the government is forced to borrow more from overseas
questions.explanation: A lower credit rating signals higher risk, so foreign demand for Australian debt and the dollars needed to buy it falls. More competitive exports would be a result of a depreciation, not its cause.

questions.stem: Currency traders expect the Australian dollar to rise and buy Australian dollars now. The effect is to:
options: increase demand for the dollar, causing it to appreciate
increase the supply of the dollar, causing it to depreciate
leave the dollar unchanged until the expected rise occurs
lower the dollar, as traders sell their Australian assets
questions.explanation: Speculative buying adds to demand for the currency, so the expected rise can bring itself about. Speculation is one reason exchange rates can move sharply in a short time.

questions.stem: Which combination is most likely to cause the Australian dollar to depreciate?
options: Rising commodity prices and higher Australian interest rates relative to overseas
Strong inflows of foreign investment and rising overseas demand for exports
An upgrade in Australia's credit rating and lower relative inflation
Falling commodity prices and lower Australian interest rates relative to overseas
questions.explanation: Lower commodity prices reduce export earnings, and lower relative interest rates reduce capital inflow, so demand for the dollar falls on both counts. Every factor in the other combinations would tend to raise the dollar.

questions.stem: A surge of foreign direct investment into Australian renewable energy projects would tend to:
options: leave the dollar unchanged, as investment flows are not part of foreign exchange
appreciate the Australian dollar, as investors buy dollars to fund the projects
depreciate the Australian dollar, as future profits will flow back overseas
depreciate the Australian dollar, as foreign investors sell Australian shares
questions.explanation: Foreign investors need Australian dollars to pay for Australian projects, so the inflow increases demand for the dollar. Profits paid overseas in the future do not offset the immediate rise in demand.

questions.stem: The terms of trade is measured as:
options: the volume of exports divided by the volume of imports, multiplied by 100
the index of import prices divided by the index of export prices, multiplied by 100
the value of exports minus the value of imports over a period
the index of export prices divided by the index of import prices, multiplied by 100
questions.explanation: The terms of trade compares the prices Australia receives for its exports with the prices it pays for imports. Volumes and the trade balance are different measures.

questions.stem: The export price index rises from 100 to 120 and the import price index rises from 100 to 105. The terms of trade index is now about:
questions.explanation: The terms of trade is 120 ÷ 105 × 100 ≈ 114.3. Dividing import prices by export prices gives 87.5, which is the ratio the wrong way round.

questions.stem: A rise in Australia's terms of trade means that:
options: the Australian dollar has depreciated against major currencies
import prices are rising faster than the prices of exports
a given volume of exports now pays for a larger volume of imports
Australia is now exporting a greater volume of goods and services
questions.explanation: A higher terms of trade means export prices have risen relative to import prices, so each unit exported buys more imports. It concerns relative prices, not the volume of exports.

questions.stem: Which of the following is most likely to cause a fall in Australia's terms of trade?
options: A fall in world prices for coal and iron ore
Lower production costs in the countries Australia imports from
A rise in global demand for liquefied natural gas
A rise in the world price of Australian wheat
questions.explanation: Coal and iron ore are major Australian exports, so a fall in their prices lowers the export price index and the terms of trade. Lower costs in supplier countries reduce import prices, which raises the terms of trade.

questions.stem: Lower production costs in the countries that supply Australia's manufactured imports would, other things being equal:
options: leave the terms of trade unchanged, as only export prices count
improve Australia's terms of trade, as import prices fall
worsen Australia's terms of trade, as import prices fall
worsen Australia's terms of trade, as export volumes fall
questions.explanation: If suppliers' costs fall, the prices Australia pays for imports tend to fall, and the denominator of the terms of trade falls. The terms of trade therefore rises, which is an improvement.

questions.stem: A sustained rise in Australia's terms of trade is most likely to:
options: lower aggregate demand, as the Australian dollar tends to depreciate
raise unemployment, as Australia's export industries tend to contract
raise national income and aggregate demand, possibly adding to inflation
lower national income, as import prices rise faster than export prices
questions.explanation: Higher export prices raise incomes for exporters, workers and government, which lifts spending and economic growth. If spending outpaces capacity, the extra demand can add to inflation; the dollar also tends to appreciate rather than fall.

questions.stem: International competitiveness refers to the ability of Australian producers to:
options: raise their export prices faster than their import prices
sell goods and services in world markets at competitive prices and quality
set the tariffs that apply to goods imported into Australia
keep the trade-weighted index above its long-run average
questions.explanation: A competitive economy can match or beat foreign producers on price and quality, at home and overseas. Raising export prices relative to import prices is an improvement in the terms of trade, a different concept.

questions.stem: Which of the following is most likely to improve Australia's international competitiveness?
options: An appreciation of the Australian dollar against major currencies
Higher inflation in Australia than in its trading partners
Productivity growth that lowers unit costs of production
Wage increases well above the rate of productivity growth
questions.explanation: Higher productivity lets firms produce at lower cost per unit, so they can offer lower prices or better quality. The other changes raise Australian prices relative to foreign prices.

questions.stem: Australia's large reserves of iron ore and natural gas affect its international competitiveness by:
options: guaranteeing that the Australian dollar will keep appreciating
reducing its productivity across all other industries
giving it a cost advantage in producing these commodities
raising its rate of inflation relative to trading partners
questions.explanation: Availability of natural resources is a source of competitiveness, because abundant, accessible deposits can be extracted at low cost. This helps make Australia a leading exporter of these commodities.

questions.stem: A large depreciation of the Australian dollar is likely to:
options: reduce economic growth, as Australian exports become dearer for foreign buyers
lower inflation, as imported goods become cheaper for Australian households
reduce the Australian dollar value of debt owed in foreign currencies
raise net exports and economic growth in the short term, but add to inflation
questions.explanation: A lower dollar makes exports cheaper and imports dearer, lifting net exports, aggregate demand and growth. It also raises import prices, adding to inflation, and increases the Australian dollar cost of foreign currency debt.

questions.stem: An appreciation of the Australian dollar is most likely to benefit:
options: Australian households buying imported goods and travelling overseas
Australian universities selling education to international students
Australian manufacturers that compete with imported products
Australian farmers selling wheat in overseas markets
questions.explanation: A stronger dollar buys more foreign currency, so imports and overseas travel become cheaper for Australians. Exporters and import-competing firms lose competitiveness, as their prices rise relative to foreign rivals.
